title: At 83, Amitabh Bachchan Still Battles Ghosts of Coolie — And the NRI World Holds Its Breath
excerpt: The Bollywood legend was quietly admitted to Mumbai's Nanavati Hospital last week for complications from a 44-year-old on-set injury. For millions of diaspora Indians, the scare was deeply personal.
body:
When Amitabh Bachchan posted a cryptic poem on his blog last Wednesday — about eagles falling silent while parrots chatter — most fans scrolled past it as vintage Big B philosophising. But behind the literary flourish lay a more sobering reality: the 83-year-old had been admitted to Nanavati Hospital in Mumbai three days earlier, on May 16, for complications traced back to the most famous accident in Indian cinema history.

## A Wound That Never Fully Healed

In 1982, during the filming of *Coolie* in Bangalore, a fight sequence with actor Puneet Issar went catastrophically wrong. A mistimed jump sent Bachchan crashing into the corner of a table, rupturing his intestine. He was rushed to hospital, where surgeons operated for hours. When the sutures ruptured days later in a Bombay hospital, a second emergency surgery followed — after which the actor could not come out of anaesthesia for 12 to 14 hours. His pulse and blood pressure dropped to near zero. Doctors declared him clinically dead.

He survived, of course, against extraordinary odds. But the injury left lasting damage — an estimated 75 per cent of his liver was compromised, and chronic abdominal issues have shadowed him for four decades. The admission last week, to the VIP enclosure on the third floor of Nanavati's A Wing, was reportedly related to these long-standing stomach complications.

## The Quiet Hospital Stay

According to journalist Vickey Lalwani, Bachchan had been in the hospital since May 16. Son Abhishek Bachchan was seen arriving at the hospital on May 19 to check on his father. Neither the Bachchan family nor their representatives issued a formal statement, though a source told NDTV the visit was for a "routine examination" and that the actor had been discharged shortly after tests were completed.

Bachchan himself offered no direct confirmation. Instead, true to form, he turned to his blog — the personal Tumblr page he has maintained for years, writing daily dispatches to his "extended family" of followers. The cryptic poem, signed off with "Love, Prayers and more," and a puzzling tweet reading "Pilori — Badumba" were the only public acknowledgements of anything unusual.

## Why NRIs Care So Deeply

For Indians living abroad, Amitabh Bachchan is not merely a film star. He is a generational anchor — the voice of *Kaun Banega Crorepati* that echoes through family WhatsApp groups, the Angry Young Man their parents watched in packed single-screen theatres in the 1970s, the cultural constant that bridges the gap between homeland and adopted country.

Every health scare involving Big B sends ripples through the diaspora that are difficult to overstate. When he tested positive for COVID-19 in 2020, NRI WhatsApp groups lit up with prayer chains and live hospital updates. The pattern repeated last week, albeit more quietly — news of the hospitalisation spread through diaspora media channels before any official word came, triggering the familiar cycle of concern, speculation, and relief.

For first-generation immigrants especially, Bachchan's health is a proxy for their own anxieties about ageing parents back home. If the seemingly invincible Big B can be felled by a 44-year-old injury, the fragility of loved ones thousands of miles away feels suddenly sharper.

## Still Working, Still Defiant

What makes the recurring health worries all the more poignant is Bachchan's relentless work ethic. At 83, his slate would exhaust actors half his age. He is set to appear in the sequel to Nag Ashwin's *Kalki 2898 AD* opposite Prabhas, in Ribhu Dasgupta's courtroom drama *Section 84* alongside Diana Penty and Nimrat Kaur, and in *Brahmastra Part Two: Dev*. Season 18 of KBC is in the works.

It is a schedule that speaks to both his extraordinary resilience and the stubborn reality of the body he inhabits — one that was, by medical consensus, supposed to have given out 44 years ago in a Bangalore hospital.

## What Comes Next

Bachchan appears to be recovering well. But each hospitalisation now arrives with an implicit question the diaspora would rather not confront: how much longer can the last of Bollywood's original titans keep defying the odds?

For now, the eagle has not fallen silent. The parrots will have to wait.
